name: Optimize the Chain — SaharaFresh's Service Collapse
description:
A four-round, advanced operations and supply-chain simulation set in SaharaFresh Distribution Ltd., a fictional Lagos-headquartered third-party FMCG distributor: ₦96bn revenue, a 4.5% EBIT margin, four distribution centres (Lagos, Ibadan, Abuja, Onitsha) and 1,400 SKUs sold into open markets, kiosks and modern trade across Nigeria. Its two largest principals, together 41% of revenue, measure on-time-in-full (OTIF) on their own lines: it stands at 78% against a 95% contract, and a clause lets them appoint a parallel distributor if it stays below 90% for a second quarter. Logistics cost runs at 16.7% of revenue, including generator power, checkpoints and levies, empty return legs and emergency transfers between DCs, against an illustrative Nigerian peer figure of about 13%. Working capital is tight: ₦0.8bn of undrawn bank line, with overdraft at 32% a year.

Playing the Head of Operations, students (1) spend 20 analyst-days on a diagnosis across lanes, demand behaviour and field ride-alongs, and decide what to do with emergency transfers and sub-wholesaler credit in the first 30 days; (2) choose a footprint, a delivery window into the open markets and a truck-fill target for the quarter the clause is measured on; (3) set safety stock for the Christmas peak, deciding the basis for segmentation, where buffers sit, two service levels and the response to a port clearing delay; and (4) choose who moves stock to the markets in 2027, how that partner is paid and held, what to invest and what goes in the 90-day plan for the principals. Each round asks for a forecast, compared with the result. Conditions vary by session (diesel price, port delays, a disruption at the Lagos DC, rail reliability), and several consequences arrive one or two rounds after the decision that caused them.

All figures are modelled and illustrative. KPIs: OTIF (%), logistics cost (% of revenue), inventory turns on cost of goods, cash headroom (₦bn) and EBIT impact (₦bn); the debrief reports an outcome and a process score, the turning point of the run and questions for class discussion. English and Spanish.
view:
14 July 2026 · SaharaFresh Distribution Ltd., Lagos · Head of Operations

Optimize the Chain

You run operations for a ₦96bn FMCG distributor with four distribution centres and a 4.5% margin. Two principals worth 41% of revenue have put the account on notice. Four rounds: the next 30 days, the rest of Q3, the Q4 peak and the first quarter of 2027.

Where the business stands

Round 1 of 4

  • OTIF, principals' lines 78% Contract 95% · clause below 90%
  • Logistics cost 16.7% % of revenue · Nigerian peers ≈13% (illustrative)
  • Inventory turns 6.5x On cost of goods · 8.3x on revenue
  • Cash headroom ₦0.80bn Undrawn bank line · overdraft at 32% a year
  • EBIT impact ₦0.00bn Annualised, vs today · base EBIT ₦4.32bn

    Round 1 · The next 30 days

    NorthStar Foods and AquaClean

    Your decisions

    How do you spend your team's 20 analyst-days?

    61% (61% today)

    A truck that waits to fill makes fewer trips, and the orders on it wait too.

    Decisions round by round

    Glossary

text.en: Diagnose the dominant cost-and-service lever among network, inventory and transport using cost-to-serve data by lane and SKU class before committing capital to a fix
Design a distribution-network footprint that minimizes total landed cost, recognizing that a saving in one cost line can be more than offset by a rise in another
Segment inventory policy by SKU class, setting the review system and cycle service level, to hit a fill-rate target and an inventory-turns target at the same time
Evaluate a logistics-outsourcing decision as a risk-transfer contract governed by a service-level agreement rather than as a rate-card comparison
Plan a recovery against a binding contractual deadline that puts near-zero-cost quick wins ahead of a multi-year structural redesign

prerequisites.en: Basic inventory and network-design concepts such as EOQ, safety stock and facility location
